title: Plasmon-Enhanced Second-Harmonic Generation in Atomically Thin Crystalline Silver Nanostructures
authors: Saad Abdullah, Philipp K. Jenke, Andrew P. Weber, Álvaro Rodríguez Echarri, Vahagn Mkhitaryan, Fadil Iyikanat, Frederik Schiller, Philip Walther, J. Enrique Ortega, Lee A. Rozema, F. Javier García de Abajo
abstract: The intrinsically weak nonlinear optical response of existing materials, further constrained by symmetry-forbidden second-order processes in centrosymmetric media, severely limits efficient frequency conversion in deeply subwavelength, ultrathin volumes. Addressing this challenge is crucial for the development of nonlinear nanophotonics. Here, we show that atomically thin, epitaxially grown crystalline silver films circumvent these restrictions through the interplay of vertical electronic quantum confinement and lateral plasmonic enhancement. We fabricate atomically thin films that exhibit an enhanced nonlinear response associated with electronic quantum wells, and subsequently pattern them into periodic nanoribbon and nanotriangle arrays sustaining infrared localized surface plasmon resonances. Strong near-field confinement in these structures further boosts second-harmonic generation compared to unpatterned films. Precise control over nanostructure geometry enables spectral tuning of the plasmonic resonance, and consequently, the enhanced harmonic frequency. Our findings establish an approach for activating robust second-order nonlinearities in quantum-confined metals, where intrinsic size effects and plasmonic resonances act synergistically. The compatibility of high-quality epitaxial growth with microchip fabrication technology offers a scalable route toward ultracompact nonlinear optical components for on-chip frequency conversion, sensing, and quantum photonic applications.
summary: This paper reports on enhancing Second-Harmonic Generation (SHG) in atomically thin crystalline silver nanostructures by exploiting two effects: quantum confinement and plasmonic resonance. By patterning the films into nanoribbons, the authors achieve a significant, tunable boost in the nonlinear optical response. This establishes a scalable method for creating compact, high-performance nonlinear components for quantum photonics.
main_problem: The weak nonlinear optical response of materials, especially those constrained by symmetry in ultrathin volumes, limits efficient frequency conversion.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that combining vertical electronic quantum confinement in atomically thin silver films with lateral plasmonic enhancement in patterned nanostructures significantly boosts Second-Harmonic Generation (SHG).
method: The study uses high-resolution electron-beam lithography to create periodic nanoribbons and nanotriangles on epitaxially grown silver films, followed by SHG measurements using ultrafast laser pulses.
model_or_system: The physical system is atomically thin, epitaxially grown crystalline silver (Ag) films, patterned into nanoribbons or triangles, and capped with gold. The enhancement mechanism relies on the synergy between quantum-well states (QWS) from thickness confinement and localized surface plasmon resonances.
key_observables: Second-Harmonic Generation (SHG) signal intensity, SHG conversion efficiency ($\eta$), and Quantum Well States (QWS) observed via ARPES.
important_parameters: Film thickness (7 to 14 monolayers), nanostructure geometry (ribbon width, period), and excitation wavelengths ($\lambda_0 = 1.98 \mu	ext{m}, 2.3 \mu	ext{m}, 3.1 \mu	ext{m}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on assuming the SHG surface susceptibility is local and independent of surface orientation when calculating enhancement ratios.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the general scheme of enhancement, ARPES data confirming QWS, SEM images of patterned structures, FTIR spectra, and plots comparing SHG enhancement factors for patterned vs. unpatterned films.
paper_structure: The work progresses by first establishing the fundamental limitation of nonlinear optics in thin films, then detailing the fabrication and characterization of patterned Ag nanostructures, and finally quantifying the synergistic enhancement of SHG due to both quantum confinement and plasmonic resonance.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it demonstrates a solid-state platform for engineering strong, tunable nonlinear optical responses at the nanoscale, which is crucial for integrated quantum photonic circuits.

General scheme illustrating the generation of an enhanced second-harmonic signal driven by vertical electronic confinement and lateral plasmonic near-field enhancement. (a) We consider atomically thin crystalline metal nanoribbons capped with gold. Pairs of incident photons at the fundamental frequency ω are converted into second-harmonic photons at frequency 2ω. The input and output light polarizations are oriented across the ribbons. FIG. 2. Spectral and geometrical dependence of SHG enhancement. (a) Scheme of the structures under consideration, consisting of Au-capped Ag-ribbon arrays (width W, period P = 3 W). (b,c) Calculated and FTIR-measured reflectance spectra for different ribbon widths. (d) Measured SHG enhancement of the ribbon arrays relative to the SHG signal of the homogeneous metal film for three different incident light wavelengths λ0 as a function of ribbon width. (e) Reflectance at the three excitation wavelengths for the same sample as in (d). Silver ribbons lie on a Si substrate, have a fixed thickness of 11 MLs of Ag(111), and are capped with 4 MLs of Au(111).

FIG. 3. Variation of SHG enhancement with Ag film thicknesses. (a-i) Experimentally measured (solid curves) and theoretically estimated (dashed curves) SHG enhancement, referenced to the corresponding unpatterned ultrathin metal film, as a function of ribbon width for different film thicknesses (7 MLs (a-c), 11 MLs (d-f), and 14 MLs (g-i) of Ag) and incident light wavelengths (λ0 = 1.98 µm (a,d,g), 2.3 µm (b,e,h), and 3.1 µm (c,f,i)). All samples are coated with 4 MLs of Au. (j-l) Measured reflectance at the SHG excitation wavelengths as a function of ribbon width for the thicknesses considered in panels (a-i) (color-coordinated curves) at the same fundamental excitation wavelengths.
